caseno: Criminal Miscellaneous Case No. 13701, 13702 of 2007 and 706 of 2008.
lawyer:
Kazi Sanwar Ahmed, Advocate—For the Petitioner. 
Dr Sharif Bhuiyan, Advocate—For the Opposite-Party No. 1.
Md Khurshedul Alam, Deputy Attorney-General and Delawar Hossain Samaddar, Assistant Attorney-General—For the State-Opposite-Party No. 2.
parties:
Nurun Nabi ----- Petitioner
 Vs
State and another ----- Opposite Parties
full_judgment:
2. These three Rules, at the instance of the accused-petitioner, were issued on the applications under section 561A of the Code of Criminal Procedure calling upon the opposite-parties to show cause as to why the Sessions Case No.1058 of 2007 arising out of CR Case 245 of 2007 (Double Mooring Zone) and Sessions Case No. 1059 of 2007 (Double Mooring Zone) arising out of CR Case No.269 of 2007 now pending before the Court of Metropolitan Sessions Judge, Chittagong and CR Case No. 420 of 2007 (Double Mooring Zone) now pending before the Court of Chief Metropolitan Magistrate, Chittagong under section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881, should not be quashed and/or pass such other or further order or orders as to this Court may seem fit and proper. 

 3. Facts leading to issuance of the Rule in Criminal Miscellaneous Case No.13701 of 2007 are as follows: 

 5. Facts relevant to disposal of the Rule issued in Criminal Miscellaneous Case No. 13702 of 2007 are as follows: 

 7. Facts necessary for the purpose of disposal of the Rule issued in Criminal Miscellaneous Case No. 706 of 2008 are as follows: 

 8. The complainant is a banking company formed and incorporated in Bangladesh under the Companies Act, 1913 and the petitioner is the proprietor of Messrs Akhter Enterprise. The accused-petitioner approached the complainant's bank for credit facilities by way of opening inland letters of credit. Accordingly, the complainant opened letters of credit and on arrival of those papers, the petitioner accepted the same; but failed to pay off the bill amount on maturity. Since the petitioner failed to pay up the bill on inland letters of credit, the complainant had to create forced time loans which stood at Taka 3,08,73,000 (Taka three crore eight lakh and seventy three thousand) with interest as on 2-8-2007 in the account of the accused-petitioner. In spite of repeated requests and reminders, the accused-petitioner did not adjust the liability, whereupon the complainant issued a legal notice to adjust the liabilities, but to no avail. The accused-petitioner, thereafter, gave two cheques being Cheque No. 4686227 dated 25-4-2007 for Taka 70,00,000 (Seventy lakhs) and Cheque No. 4686228 dated 25-5-2007 for Taka 30,00,000 (Thirty lakhs) to the complainant both drawn on Sonali Bank, Mithagali Branch, Dewanhat, Chittagong. Both the cheques were presented on different dates; but they were dishonoured. Cheque No. 4686227 dated 25-4-2007 was again presented on 20-8-2007 for encashment; but it was dishonoured on the ground of 'insufficient funds'. Cheque No. 4686228 dated 25-5-2007 was also lastly presented on 20-8-2007 for encashment, but the same was dishonoured for "Insufficient funds". The complainant, thereafter, issued a legal notice with registered A/D to the accused-petitioner through its lawyer on 2-9-2007 demanding the payment of Taka 3,08,73,000 (Taka three crore eight lakh and seventy three thousands); but the said legal notice was not received in collusion with the postal peon and no payment was made relating to the cheque amount. Hence, the case against the accused-petitioner under section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881. 

 9. On receipt of the petitions of complainant, the learned Metropolitan Magistrate, Chittagong examined the complainant under section 200 of the Code of Criminal Procedure and after being satisfied, the learned Metropolitan Magistrate issued summons upon the accused-petitioner directing him to appear before the Court. The accused-petitioner voluntarily surrendered before the Court and submitted an application for bail, whereupon the learned Metropolitan Magistrate enlarged him on bail and subsequently, the case records of CR Case No. 245 of 2007 and CR Case No. 269 of 2007 were sent to the Metropolitan Sessions Judge, Chittagong for trail. 

 10. On receiving the case records, the learned Metropolitan Sessions Judge, Chittagong, on consideration of the prosecution materials and on hearing the parties, took cognizance of the offence against the accused-petitioner under section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act. 

 11. It may be noted that in CR Case No. 420 of 2007, the Chief Metropolitan Magistrate took cognizance of the offence against the accused-petitioner under section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act and the same is pending thereto. 

 13. No one appears on behalf of the accused-petitioner to press the Rule at the time of taking up the same for hearing. However, the accused-petitioner filed these miscellaneous cases before this Court on some grounds which may be, briefly, stated as follows:— 

 IV. For that the impugned proceedings are not sustainable in law as the complainant filed the petitions of complaint before expiry of mandatory waiting period of "thirty days" from the date of receipt of legal notices as stipulated in Clause (c) of the Proviso to section 138 and the learned Courts below took cognizance of the offences in the instant cases in gross violation of the mandatory provisions of section 141 of the said Act before the accrual of the cause of action. 

 14. On the other hand, Mr Dr Sharif Bhuiyan, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of opposite-party No. 1, submits that the petitions of complaint contain prima-facie offences against the petitioner under section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 and, as such, the impugned proceedings should not be quashed. He next submits that though the petitions of complaint were filed before accrual of the cause of action, the accused-petitioner did not take any step for payment of the said cheque amount and, as such, the impugned proceedings are maintainable in spite of the fact that the petitions of complaint were filed before expiry of 30 days from the date of receipt of notice. He then submits that though the petitions of complaint were filed before accrual of the cause of action, the same are maintainable and that the same cannot be circumvented by any technicality of law and, as such, the impugned proceedings should be quashed. Learned Advocate, in support of his submission, relied on the decisions in the cases of Veeraraghavan vs Lalith Kumar, reported in MANU/TN/0195/1994, Sarwar Hossain Mani vs State reported in 16 BLC (AD) 71, Satya Narayan Poddar vs State reported in 53 DLR 403 and Sirajul Islam vs Tauhid Uddin Ahmed reported in 15 BLC 39. 

 17. In view of the submissions made by the learned Advocate for opposite-party No. 1 and on consideration of the other prosecution materials on record, a question arises whether the impugned proceedings should be quashed. In order to appreciate the same, it will be necessary to see the principles and categories of cases in which the High Court Division may invoke its power and authority under section 561A of the Code of Criminal Procedure. 

 18. In the decision in the case of Abdul Quader Chowdhury vs State, 28 DLR (AD) 38, it has been held that the High Court Division may quash a criminal proceeding invoking its jurisdiction under section 561A of the Code of Criminal Procedure in the following circumstances:— 

 (1) Interference even at an initial stage may be justified where the facts are so preposterous that even on admitted facts no case stands against the accused. 

 (4) In a case where the allegations in the FIR or the petition of complaint, even if taken at their face value and accepted in their entirety, do not constitute the offence as alleged. 

 (5) The allegations against the accused although constitute an offence alleged but there is either no legal evidence adduced in support of the case or the evidence adduced clearly or manifestly fails to prove the charge. 

 19. Similar view, on the principles and categories of cases for quashing the proceedings, was, subsequently, taken in many decisions in the cases of Ali Akkas vs Enayet Hossain, 17 BLD (AD) 44 = 2 BLC (AD) 16, and Bangladesh vs Tan Khen Hock, 31 DLR (AD) 69. 

 20. It is pertinent to note that the inherent power under section 561A of the Code of Criminal Procedure can be invoked at any stage of the proceedings even after conclusion of the trial, if it is necessary to prevent the abuse of the process of the Court or otherwise to secure the ends of justice. In the decisions in the case of Sher Ali vs State, 46 DLR (AD) 67 it has been decided that the inherent power under section 561A of the Code of Criminal Procedure can be exercised to quash a proceedings or even a conviction on conclusion of a trial if the Court concerned got no jurisdiction to hold the said trial or the facts alleged against the accused do not constitute any criminal offence, or the conviction has been based on 'no evidence' or otherwise to secure ends of justice. 

 21. Reverting to the present cases, it transpires that the accused-petitioner issued a number of cheques in favour of the complain-ant in order to pay up the bill arising out of inland letters of credit. Almost all the cheques bounced for insufficient funds; but one of the cheques was returned unpaid with the endorsement 'present again'. One of the grounds taken in the application under section 561A of the Code of Criminal Procedure is that since the alleged cheque having not been returned by the bank for the reasons as contemplated by section 138 of the Act, the return of the cheque with the endorsement 'present again' does not fall within the ambit of bouncing of cheque under section 138 of the Act. 

 23. In support of the aforesaid submissions, the learned Advocate for opposite-party No. 1 referred to a decision in the case of Veeraraghavan vs Lalith Kumar reported in MANU/TN/0195/1994, wherein it has been held in paragraph No. 14. 

 "The English language is not an instrument of mathematical precision. Our literature would be much poorer if it were. This is where the draftsmen of Acts of Parliament have often been unfairly criticized. A Judge, believing himself to be fettered by the supposed rule that he must look to the language and nothing else, laments that the draftsmen have not provided for this or that, or have been guilty of some or other ambiguity. It would certainly save the Judges trouble if the Acts of Parliament were drafted with divine prescience and perfect clarity. In the absence of it, when a defect appears a Judge cannot simply fold his hands and blame the draftsmen. He must set to work on the constructive task of finding the intention of Parliament, and he must do this not only from the language of the statute but also from a consideration of the social conditions which gave rise to it and of the mischief which it was passed to remedy, and then he must supplement the written word so as to give force and life to the intention of Legislature. A Judge should ask himself the question how, if the makers of the Act had themselves come across this ruck in the texture of it, they would have straightened it our? He must then do so they would have done. A Judge must not alter the material of which the Act is woven, but he can and should iron out the creases." 

 26. By referring to the aforesaid decisions, it is contended by the learned Advocate for opposite-party No. 1 that though the words 'present again' are not included in the statute so as to express the exact meaning of bouncing of cheque in view of section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, this Court may come forward in construing an Act with an aid of the rule of purposive construction or mischief rule in order to find out the intention of Legislature and supplement the written words so as to give force and life to the intention of the Legislature. 

 28. It is undisputed that the legislative intent and purpose of enactment of the Act is to prevent the offences mentioned thereto and render social justice against the mischief allegedly committed by an offender or offenders. In this regard, it is incumbent upon a Judge to consider the social condition and think of the remedy to be given to an aggrieved person or persons against the mischief allegedly perpetrated by an accused or the accused-persons. In the absence of appropriate wording in the Act to give effect to the law, the judges of this Court may unfold their hands and set to work on the constructive tasks of finding the intention of the Parliament. In other words, in order to deal with the problems or understand a confused situation, a Judge should not make changes to the texture of the law; rather he can interpret the same so as to give effect to the law. 

 29. in the instant case, as we see it, the cheque that was presented before the bank for encashment was returned unpaid with an endorsement "present again" giving rise to the meaning that the cheque was ultimately dishonoured. 

 32. Coming back to the present case, it appears from the petitions of complaint that the accused-petitioner issued a number of cheques in favour of complainant-opposite party No. 2 who, in due course of time, presented the same before the bank for encashment; but the same was dishonoured for insufficient funds. After bouncing of the cheques, the complainant issued legal notices upon the accused-petitioner who avoided payment of the cheque amount inspite of legal notices issued by the complainant. It may be pointed out that the complainant issued a legal notice upon the petitioner on 16-5-2007 requesting the accused-petitioner to pay up the cheque amount against cheque No. 4686225 dated 25-2-2007 and cheque No. 4686224 dated 25-1-2007 and the accused-petitioner received the same on 21-5-2007; but the complainant filed the petition of complaint on 19-6-2007. It may be mentioned further that the complainant issued legal notice upon the accused-petitioner for payment of the cheque amount against cheque No. 4686226 dated 25-3-2007 on 6-6-2007 and the said legal notice was received by the accused-petitioner on 7-6-2007 and 13-6-2007 respectively; but the complainant instituted the petition of complaint on 4-7-2007. We also find that the complainant issued legal notice upon the accused-petitioner for payment of the cheque amount against cheque No. 4686227 dated 25-4-2007 and cheque No. 4686228 dated 25-5-2007 and the said notices were not received in collusion with the postal peon; but the complainant filed the petition of complaint on 2-10-2007, that is to say, before expiry of 30 days from the date of receipt of the legal notice. 

 Section 138 (b):— "The payee or the holder in due course of the cheque, as the case may be, makes a demand for the payment of the said amount of money by giving a notice, in writing, to the drawer of the cheque, within thirty days of the receipt of information by him from the bank regarding the return of the cheque as unpaid." 

 Section 138(c)— "The drawer of such cheque fails to make the payment of the said amount of money to the payee or, as the case may be, to the holder in due course of the cheque, within thirty days of the receipt to the said notice." 

 36. In order to substantiate the submissions, the learned Advocate for opposite-party No. 1, in support of his submissions, banked upon a decision in the case of Sarwar Hossain Moni vs State reported in 16 BLC (AD) 71, wherein it has been held: 

 37. In the decision in the case of Satya Narayan Poddar vs State reported in 53 DLR (2001) 403 relied upon by the learned Advocate for the opposite-party No. 1, it has been laid down: 

 "Even though the case is pre-mature and it was filed before the expiry of 15 days from the date of receipt of the notice, the proceeding is not liable to be quashed." 

 38. In the decision in the case of Sirajul Islam vs Tauhid Uddin Ahmed reported in 15 BLC 39 adverted to by the learned Advocate for opposite-party No. 1, it has been decided: 

 "In the instant case, the complaint was filed before the statutory period. The accused-petitioner did not make any payment of the amount of the cheque after the receipt of the notice nor did he take any step to make payment of the said amount in the subsequent time which clearly shows that the accused-petitioner had no intention to make the payment of the said amount. Considering this fact of the matter, it cannot be said that the legal right of the accused-petitioner had been infringed." 

 39. Under the given scenario of the case, we should consider the legislative import and intent of enactment of law regarding bouncing of the cheque. 

 40. The purpose and object of enactment of law is to combat and prevent the offences disclosed in the enacted law. In order to find out the import and intent of the enactment, the provisions of the Act should be interpreted in such a way and manner in keeping with the intention of the Legislature so that the law can adequately serve the purposes and effectively deals with the offences. It should be borne in mind that the substantive justice should not be frustrated or otherwise defeated for any technicality in the law. It is evident from the petitions of complaint that the accused-petitioner issued number of cheques in favour of the complainant who, in due course, presented the same for encashment; but the same bounced. The complainant issued notices upon the accused-petitioner who denied payment of the cheque amount. The complainant thereafter filed the petitions of complaint before the competent Court having jurisdiction. It may be mentioned here that the accused-petitioner even after filing of petitions of complaint did not make any payment of the cheque amount; rather the accused-petitioner appeared in the proceedings and on being enlarged on bail, he did not take any step for payment of the cheque amount. Under the circumstances, it can be easily presumed that had the accused-petitioner the intention to pay off the cheque amount, he could have done so during the pendency of the proceedings; but he conspicuously remained silent about the payment of the cheque amount. In the decision in the case of Satya Narayan Poddar vs State reported in 53 DLR 403, it has been held that though the petition of complaint was filed before the expiry of 30 days from the date of receipt of legal notice, the impugned proceedings are not liable to be quashed on the ground of pre-maturity of the cause of action. The aforesaid legal view has been, subsequently, endorsed by the Appellate Division in the case of Sarwar Hossain Moni vs State reported in 16 BLC (AD) 71, wherein it has been decided to the effect that a proceeding cannot be quashed on the ground of pre-maturity of the cause of action, even if the petitions of complaint were filed before the expiry of 30 days from the date of receipt of the legal notices. 

 42. From the foregoing discussions and having regard to the facts and circumstances of the case, we are led to hold that the impugned proceedings initiated against the accused-petitioner under section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 cannot be circumvented merely on the fact that the petitions of complaint were not filed before the Court after the expiry of 30 days from the date of receipt of the legal notices. 

 46. The learned Judges of the trial Court are directed to proceed with the trial of the cases in accordance with law.
